To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the three species we studied responded to UV-B radiation in a manner that suggests a high level of UV-B tolerance and that this tolerance was associated with a range of responses that may be important to their survival in a UV-B enriched environment.

1) the three species studied had different patterns of response to supplemental UV radiation, 2) the three species had different patterns of accumulation of UV-absorbing foliar compounds and 3) the three species did not show significant decreases in net photosynthesis or increases in foliar injury.

1) foliar chemistry of three eastern tree taxa responded to supplemental UV-B in different ways, 2) epidermal accumulation was the most important response to UV-B and 3) the physiological effects of UV-B radiation in this study were subtle and did not result in reduced photosynthetic efficiency or reduced productivity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the effects of UV-B radiation on forest tree species and how this might influence their ability to survive in a future world of increased UV-B radiation.
the effects of supplemental UVB on the physiology, morphology, and growth of eastern tree species.
the effects of increased UV-B radiation levels on three eastern tree species.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
UV-screening compounds are important in the UV-B tolerance of these tree species and that they may be important in the ecology of these trees in a natural environment.

the effects of supplemental UV-A and UVB on photosynthetic efficiency, gas exchange and foliar chemistry were not consistent among the three species studied and that the responses to UV-A and UV-A + UV-B were not consistent among species.

the species studied in this investigation are not sensitive to the levels of UV-B irradiance that were applied and the species studied in the investigation are able to utilize a variety of UV-screening mechanisms to achieve tolerance to UV-B irradiance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

UV-B radiation has the potential to influence the physiology of these tree species and that the effects of UV-B radiation on photosynthesis and gas exchange are not consistent with the hypothesis that UV-B radiation is a stressor.
these three species were tolerant of UV-B exposure and that they used a variety of mechanisms to attenuate the effects of UV-B radiation.

UV-B radiation had little influence on photosynthesis and leaf area in mature trees of these three species, but did have some influence on stomatal conductance and WUE, which could have ecological implications.
The main takeaway from our work is that
UV-B radiation can be an important factor influencing plant performance and that this may occur in the absence of visible damage to leaves or reduced growth.

the effects of UV-B on plant productivity and physiology are complex, and the response of individual species to UV-B radiation is dependent on the suite of UV-screening mechanisms that are present and their effectiveness in attenuating UV-B.
there are many ways to deal with UV-B and that the physiological effects may be more important than the amount of damage to photosystem II.
